source: Bizer & Petty (2005) How we conceptualize our attitudes matters, Study 1
finding: Founding study. 69 Ohio State undergraduates read about two fictitious county commissioner candidates, picked a preference freely, then were asked 'what do you think about X being elected?' for either candidate. That wording made a person with the same preference either a supporter of the liked one or an opposer of the disliked one. A message attacking the preferred candidate followed. Opposers changed less.
numbers: Attitude change (oppose vs support): M = 2.42 vs 3.69, F(1,59)=3.99, p=.05. 10 of 69 removed. Initial attitudes did not differ by condition (F<1).
quote: Merely conceptualizing one's preferences as opposing something will make that preference more resistant to persuasion
limits: Borderline p (.05). Small student sample. Fictitious low-involvement candidates. Resistance measured on one message; mechanism untested.
agent_relevance: Same position, different wording gives different downstream strength. An agent that restates a problem as 'reject X' vs 'accept Y' may change its own commitment. S1 neutral restatement should strip the frame.

source: Bizer & Petty (2005) Study 2: priming control and match/mismatch design
finding: Tested whether the opposition effect is just negativity priming. Participants framed attitudes toward political candidates, then faced a message about the same candidates (match) or about a different pair, library job applicants (mismatch). If it were priming, resistance would spread to the unrelated message. It did not.
numbers: Framing x Match interaction F(1,86)=15.45, p<.001. Match: F(1,43)=16.10, p<.001. Mismatch: F(1,43)=1.37, ns. Match cell attitude change: opposers 1.40 vs supporters 2.92, F(1,43)=12.45, p=.001. About 90 analysed after removing 10.
quote: participants in the 'mismatch' condition showed no effect of initial attitude framing on subsequent attitudes
limits: Effect is object-specific, not a general mood. N for Study 2 not stated outright; df imply about 90.
agent_relevance: The frame acts on the framed object only. A frame set for one sub-question should not leak to others; a reset between S-states is enough.

source: Bizer & Petty (2005) Study 3: relative preference on a bipolar scale
finding: 22 Eastern Illinois students, one candidate described as clearly better. Everyone rated on the same 9-point bipolar scale before and after an attack on the favored candidate, so measure mismatch cannot explain the result. Opposers still moved less.
numbers: Change in relative preference: oppose M=2.36 vs support M=4.00, F(1,20)=5.40, p=.03. N=22.
limits: Tiny N (22). One candidate pair. No replication of the Study 3 design in the opened papers.
agent_relevance: Fragile in size, but direction held in all three studies. Treat as a small-to-medium, context-bound effect.

source: Bizer & Petty (2005) Discussion: proposed mechanisms
finding: Authors propose a two-step account: negative framing raises certainty, then certainty raises resistance. Candidate sources of certainty: bivariate attitude model (negative attitudes need more information than positive ones), more cognitive activity for negatives, negativity bias. Three ELM routes to resistance: rejection cue, less careful processing, more counterarguing.
numbers: No mediation test in the 2005 paper.
quote: the mediational process underlying this effect remains unknown
limits: Mechanism was speculation in 2005. Later work tests certainty (2011), depth of processing (2013), ambivalence and disambiguation (2025-26).
agent_relevance: The agent analogue of certainty is stated confidence. Framing may raise confidence without adding evidence; confidence is not a check (G3).

source: Bizer, Larsen & Petty (2011) Exploring the valence-framing effect, Experiment 1
finding: 70 train-station adults read about two fictitious state supreme court candidates (one Republican, one Democrat). Asked 'support or oppose' one candidate by random assignment. Opposers (opposing the other party) were more certain than supporters. Number of thoughts listed did not differ.
numbers: Certainty: opposers M=4.90 (SD 1.82) vs supporters M=4.17 (SD 1.96), F(1,58)=7.94, partial eta2=.07. Thoughts: 2.13 vs 1.92, F<1. 7 inconsistent and 1 missing removed.
limits: Paper prints p=.04 beside F(1,58)=7.94, which would normally be p<.01; likely a typo, flag when citing. Convenience sample.
agent_relevance: Framing changed certainty without changing the amount of thinking: the effect is metacognitive, not extra reasoning. Warning for any step that asks the model for confidence.

source: Bizer, Larsen & Petty (2011) Experiment 2: real election, certainty and intentions
finding: Representative panel (Knowledge Networks) in New Jersey and Virginia gubernatorial races, 1-15 weeks before the 2005 election. 471 adults, 451 kept. Random assignment to say support or oppose for one major-party candidate. Among the 290 who truly preferred one candidate, opposers were more certain and had stronger behavioural intentions. Among the 161 with no preference there was no effect.
numbers: Certainty (1-5) with preference: opposers 3.90 vs supporters 3.43, F(1,442)=15.51, p<.001, partial eta2=.04. No preference: 2.56 vs 2.48, F<1. Intentions with preference: 3.05 vs 2.76, F(1,442)=11.08, p=.001, partial eta2=.02. Framing x Preference on certainty F=4.00, p=.046; on intentions F(1,442)=9.52, p=.002.
limits: Effect needs a real preference where oppose-A equals support-B. Effect sizes small (eta2 .02-.04). Discussion mentions donating money though only voting, persuading and volunteering were measured.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: the frame only bites when the binary is exclusive. Mirrors our rule that answer sets must be exclusive before normalising (G5).

source: Bizer, Larsen & Petty (2011) mediation: certainty carries framing into behaviour
finding: Baron-Kenny and Sobel mediation on the 290 with a preference. Framing raised certainty, certainty raised intentions, and the framing effect on intentions vanished once certainty was controlled.
numbers: Framing->certainty b=0.27, t(289)=4.75; framing->intentions b=0.19, t(289)=3.19, p=.002; certainty->intentions b=.60, t(289)=12.80; framing controlling certainty b=0.02, ns; Sobel z=4.43, p<.001. Certainty-intentions r=.59.
limits: Cross-sectional mediation; mediator and outcome both measured after the manipulation. The 2026 Rovenpor work found no confidence mediation for willingness to pay.
agent_relevance: Certainty is the lever. If our agent reports certainty after a frame, that number is contaminated by the frame.

source: Bizer, Larsen & Petty (2011) positioning: from inoculation to metacognition
finding: Places valence framing against McGuire's inoculation theory (needs effortful counterarguing) and Rucker, Petty & Briñol (2008), where labelling a bicycle's attributes 'pros and cons' (two-sided frame) raised certainty with attitudes unchanged. Valence framing is another cheap metacognitive route to strength. Notes survey implication: 'anti-abortion' vs 'pro-life' wording could change willingness to act.
numbers: Rucker et al. 2008 and McGuire & Papageorgis 1961 described, not re-run.
quote: Valence framing thus appears to be a relatively low-effort way to impact multiple features associated with strong attitudes.
limits: Rucker 2008 and Tormala & Petty 2002 are secondhand here (originals not opened).
agent_relevance: Wording-only manipulations of perceived evidence breadth can raise confidence. Neutral restatement removes pros/cons labels and support/oppose verbs.

source: Bizer, Larsen & Petty (2011) Experiment 2 data cleaning and null on extremity
finding: Attitude extremity did not differ by support/oppose, candidate asked about, or preference, so the framing leaves the position itself untouched. Preference vs none: certainty 3.67 vs 2.51, F(1,442)=142.55, partial eta2=.24. Framing main effect on certainty 3.21 vs 2.96, F(1,442)=6.75, p=.01, partial eta2=.02.
numbers: Exclusions 20 of 471 (4.2%). Preference 290 (64.3%), no preference 161 (35.7%): 136 'none', 25 'someone else'. Share saying 'support' ranged 35.7% (Forrester) to 66.7% (Corzine).
limits: Effect on certainty overall is small (eta2 .02). 'Preference' is classified after the framing question.
agent_relevance: The answer can look unchanged while strength changes: check confidence and stability, not only the answer, when testing frames.

source: Taylor (2018) Choosing between similarly (un)desirable options, Ohio State senior thesis, Study 1
finding: Extension, 2x2 design: candidate information valence (both positive or both negative) by support vs oppose mindset, then choice. 170 undergraduates. Confidence was highest when information was positive, the frame was support and the decision was 'choose' (a three-way match). Oppose is not always stronger.
numbers: N=170 (Study 1), 343 (Study 2), 398 (Study 3). Study 3 confidence: three-variable match M=5.243 (choice) and 5.500 (reject) vs no-frame two-way match 4.971 and 5.433.
limits: Undergraduate thesis, not peer reviewed. Frame effects interact with whether the person is choosing or rejecting.
agent_relevance: Frame x task match: a support frame fits 'pick the best', an oppose frame fits 'eliminate'. Elimination steps in our schema may inherently carry oppose framing.

source: Taylor (2018) Studies 2-3: partial replication failure and atypical cell
finding: Study 3 did not replicate the Mindset Frame x Information Valence interaction found in Studies 1 and 2. The author blames one unusually confident cell (positive information, oppose frame, choose). Unframed participants defaulted to the matching frame. Confidence mediation of the interaction was not significant.
numbers: Study 3: no replication of frame x valence interaction. Mediation of the interaction via confidence: direct b=.12, t(262)=1.347, p=.179; indirect 95% CI [-.045, .104]. Mismatch contrast with outlier cell excluded F(1,135)=4.673, p=.032; included F(1,167)=1.811, p=.18.
limits: Post hoc outlier explanation; thesis, so low weight. Shows the interaction is unstable.
agent_relevance: Effect unstable once options are similar in quality. Do not build a rule on 'oppose is stronger'; build one that removes frame wording.

source: Bizer, Zezelj & Luguri (2013) When are support and opposition not opposites? (via press release)
finding: Press release for BJSP 52:191-201. Fictional liberal and conservative candidates for a government board. Certainty effect appeared for a local board but not a distant one. Experiment 2: opposers more certain than supporters only when able and motivated to think carefully. Experiment 3: effect extended to perceived importance.
numbers: No numbers in the release. Taylor thesis and Wikipedia add that a memory load manipulation (remember a number sequence) nullified the effect.
quote: when people are not motivated and able, the effect goes away
limits: Opened only the press release, not the paper; the publisher PDF was blocked. Numbers unverified.
agent_relevance: Opposite of the usual bias story: careful processing amplifies this one. So 'think harder' will not fix a frame; only removing the frame will.

source: Zezelj et al. (2007) Valence framing of political preferences and resistance to persuasion
finding: Cited in Bizer et al. (2011) as an additional replication of the 2005 resistance effect. Original not opened (ResearchGate blocked).
numbers: Not available.
limits: Unverified secondhand citation.
agent_relevance: Independent replication exists but its numbers are still needed.

source: Catapano & Tormala (2021) Do I support that it's good or oppose that it's bad? JPSP 121(1):23-42
finding: Ten studies (7 experiments, 2 correlational, 1 field). Support-framed attitudes are shared more than oppose-framed ones, because support seems more value-expressive and makes a better impression. Effect weakens when impression-management goals are relaxed.
numbers: Study counts only; participant numbers are not on the abstract page.
limits: Only the abstract page was read. Shows 'support' can win on a different outcome (sharing) while 'oppose' wins on strength.
agent_relevance: Framing effects flip by outcome. Do not generalise from one outcome.

source: Rovenpor, Teeny & Petty (2026) Decision, Studies 1-2: opposition effect needs equal extremity
finding: Consumer version: choose between two speakers via reviews; prefer one. Framed support vs oppose, crossed with relative extremity (preferred option more extreme, nonpreferred more extreme, equal). Willingness to pay was higher under opposition ONLY when the liked option was as good as the other was bad. 459+722 MTurk workers recruited, 857 retained.
numbers: WTP equal extremity: oppose M=59.14 vs support M=45.24 (diff $13.90), F(1,840)=8.71, p=.003 (reported partial eta2=.030). Other extremity conditions p=.401 and p=.937. Disambiguity contrast F(1,840)=7.71, p=.006; matching contrast F=0.291, p=.590. Choice confidence contrast F(1,830)=3.33, p=.068 (trend; ceiling effect).
limits: Not preregistered. MTurk consumer scenarios. Confidence effect only a trend. Reported partial eta2 for the simple effect looks high versus the F; check the supplement.
agent_relevance: Strong boundary condition: the effect is largest where evidence is ambiguous about whether the choice rests on liking A or disliking B. That is the agent's typical situation on near ties.

source: Rovenpor, Teeny & Petty (2026) Study 3 and mediation tests
finding: 117 MTurk participants rated what their preference rests on, with no frame given. Positive-more-extreme: preference based on liking the better speaker (6.49); negative-more-extreme: based on disliking the worse speaker (4.61); equal: 5.56. Supports the disambiguity idea. Confidence did not mediate the framing effect on WTP.
numbers: Basis rating 6.49 vs 4.61, p<.001, d=.75; equal vs positive-more p=.088, d=.40; equal vs negative-more p=.097, d=.38. Moderated mediation via confidence: index CI [-0.51, 0.71], no mediation. N=117 after exclusions from 154.
limits: Study 3 is on perceived basis only. The mediation null contradicts the 2011 certainty account for this outcome.
agent_relevance: Stated confidence is not a reliable readout of the frame's effect; use counted checks, not stated confidence.

source: Rovenpor et al. (2026) Introduction: prior literature summary and competing accounts
finding: Summarises that support-oppose framing so far shows strength effects on confidence, resistance and voting intention, not on the preference itself. Lists candidate mechanisms: matching, negativity dominance, disambiguity. Notes the opposite sharing effect of Catapano & Tormala.
numbers: No new numbers.
limits: Review by the original authors, so framing tends toward their account.
agent_relevance: Preference direction unchanged, strength changed: exactly the pattern S1 must prevent.

source: Teeny & Petty (2025) Opposer's loss effect, JPSP, program overview
finding: Across lab, longitudinal and archival studies (N=12,830), people who frame a preference as opposing the other option react more negatively to the undesired outcome (their favourite loses) even with equal preference extremity. Mediated by lower felt ambivalence more than by certainty.
numbers: Total N=12,830. Pilot N=201: 58% self-reported framing political ads' preferences as opposition. Experiments 3-6 plus 8 supplementary studies.
limits: Mixed methods; archival and longitudinal parts lack random assignment. Authors say so.
agent_relevance: Frames shape the reaction to being wrong. An agent that framed itself as opposing an answer may overreact or entrench when told it failed. Frame-free restatement reduces this.

source: Teeny & Petty (2025) mega-analysis and meta-analysis of the manipulation
finding: Pooled all their experiments (4 primary plus 8 supplementary). Framing did not change how strongly people preferred one option; it did change negative reactions to the undesired outcome.
numbers: Preference extremity: oppose 82.92 vs support 82.70, F(1,2415)=.06, p=.804. Negative reactions: oppose M=32.14 vs support 39.51 on the study scale (lower = more negative), F(1,2415)=41.10, p<.001, partial eta2=.017. Random-effects meta d=-.284, SE .04, 95% CI [-.364, -.203].
limits: Single-paper meta-analysis by the effect's authors; no outside replication.
agent_relevance: Best current effect size for the family: d about .28. Small. Extremity untouched, so framing alters strength not the answer.

source: Teeny & Petty (2025) Studies 3-4: certainty weak, ambivalence strong
finding: Study 3 (127 undergraduates, 14 excluded): opposition cut felt ambivalence significantly, certainty only directionally. Study 4 (203 MTurk, 151 after exclusions): both moved. Preregistered Studies 5-6 show the effect shrinks for people low in ambivalence (Study 6 N=335).
numbers: Study 3 certainty oppose 6.14 vs support 5.84, F(1,109)=2.15, p=.146; ambivalence 1.79 vs 2.40, F(1,109)=6.69, p=.011. Study 4 certainty 6.37 vs 6.00, F(1,149)=5.04, p=.026; ambivalence 2.70 vs 3.44, F(1,149)=4.46, p=.036.
limits: Study 3 certainty failed to reach significance, so the 2011 certainty claim is only partly replicated. One-tailed power calculation used.
agent_relevance: Failed-in-part replication of the certainty mediator. Felt ambivalence (conflict) may be the better account: oppose framing hides the pros of the option.

source: Teeny & Petty (2025) Study 7: ChatGPT 4.0 used to code support vs oppose framing in tweets
finding: Archival Super Bowl 46 tweets. ChatGPT 4.0 classified each pregame tweet as support, opposition or uncategorizable. Only the broad support/oppose label was usable; team attribution was not.
numbers: Human check on 300 tweets: 91.4% agreement with ChatGPT on the broad support vs opposition label. Identifying which team was opposed was inaccurate, so that planned analysis was dropped.
limits: Only a labelling use of an LLM, not a test of LLM susceptibility. One model, one sample of 300.
agent_relevance: An LLM can detect frame polarity (91%) but not its target. A frame detector should flag polarity words, then code should check the target.

source: Siev, Rovenpor & Petty (2024) Independents, not partisans, hold negativity-based preferences, JESP 110:104538
finding: Five studies, N=51,687. Self-labelled independents base choices more on opposition than partisans do: more 'against' votes, and they agree more with oppose-framed appeals; partisans agree more with support-framed appeals. A person-by-frame matching effect.
numbers: Study 1 ANES 1968-2020 N=42,940; Study 2 N=7,896, 'against' voting higher among independents in 2000, 2008, 2016, 2020 (2020 chi2(1)=114.01). Study 4 combined N=557: partisanship x frame F(1,545)=12.54, p<.001, partial eta2=.023; frame main effect F=3.69, p=.055.
limits: Observational for studies 1-3 and 5. Study 4 interaction is a matching effect, not a main effect. A simple effect for low-positivity people is only p=.064.
agent_relevance: Frame effects depend on the reader's baseline. A sceptical vs supportive prior on a claim may change how a wording lands. Neutral restatement avoids matching games.

source: Wikipedia, Framing effect (psychology): valence framing summary
finding: Says Bizer, Larsen, Petty (2011) supports the original finding and Bizer, Zezelj, Luguri found depth of processing moderates: stronger when motivated and unloaded, weaker with load. It gives no sample sizes.
numbers: None.
quote: Statements oriented negatively ('I oppose') result in greater levels of attitude resistance and certainty.
limits: Secondary source. All replications so far come from the Bizer-Petty network (Ohio State, Union College, plus Zezelj in Belgrade). No independent preregistered multi-lab replication found.
agent_relevance: Evidence base is narrow and mostly one lab family. Weight accordingly.

source: Dubois et al. (2026) Ask don't tell: reducing sycophancy in LLMs (UK AISI)
finding: Not support/oppose valence directly, but the closest controlled LLM study of input framing. 440 content-matched prompts (40 yes/no questions x 11 variants: question, statement, belief, conviction, I-perspective vs user-perspective, affirm vs negate). Questions gave near-zero sycophancy; more certainty in the user's wording gave more agreement.
numbers: Bayesian GLM estimates: plain statements -0.14, beliefs 0.72, convictions 0.82 (e.g. beliefs 95% HPDI [0.68,0.75]). Models: GPT-4o 0.90, Sonnet-4.5 -0.24, GPT-5 -0.66. Graders GPT-5 and Sonnet-4.5 differ in absolute scale (-0.72 vs +0.72).
quote: questions elicit substantially lower sycophancy than non-question inputs expressing the same underlying claims
limits: Single turn, synthetic prompts, LLM-judged. Topics: hobbies, relationships, mental health, medical. Newer models much less sycophantic.
agent_relevance: Direct support for S1: converting an assertion into a neutral question lowers conformity.

source: Dubois et al. (2026) mitigation: rewrite as a question before answering
finding: Instructing the model to rephrase non-questions as questions before answering cut sycophancy more than the explicit 'do not be sycophantic' prompt. Two-step (rephrase, then answer) beat one-step. Third-person rewrite ('the user believes') gave only small reductions.
numbers: Sycophancy score: no mitigation 1.13 [1.10,1.15]; 1-step question reframing 0.16 [0.14,0.19]; 2-step question reframing -0.55 [-0.58,-0.53].
limits: Same caveats. Rewriting may cause evasive answers where validation is appropriate (authors' caution).
agent_relevance: Strong evidence for S1 as a program-run step: restate the item as a neutral question, then answer. Prefer the two-step form.

source: Kaur (2025) Echoes of agreement: argument driven sycophancy in LLMs, Findings of EMNLP 2025
finding: LLMs move toward whichever side the added argument supports. 62 Political Compass propositions, GPT-4-written supporting and refuting arguments, four open models (DeepSeek-R1, Llama-3.2, Command-R, Mistral), 10 runs each, single-turn and multi-turn flip settings. Models flip stance when given a contrary argument; some topics are stubborn. IBM-ArgQ (30,497 arguments, 71 propositions) used to vary argument strength.
numbers: 62 propositions x 4 models x 10 runs. Stance mapped to -2..+2. Directional agreement with support and refute arguments is high in all models; exact table values not extracted.
limits: No oppose-vs-support wording manipulation, only argument direction. Open mid-size models only; no frontier models.
agent_relevance: Shows that framing text moves LLM stance. Supports G2 and G4: do not let a prompt's stance steer a revision; revise only from real failing output.

source: Bizer & Petty (2005) design logic and the Bush-supporter vs Kerry-opposer analogy
finding: Core inference logic: randomly split equally pro-A people; one half answers 'what do you think of A being elected', the other 'what do you think of B being elected'. Information and preference are the same; only the label differs. The frame is imposed by question wording, not by instruction.
numbers: Study 1 used a 2-point support/oppose answer plus an 11-point continuous attitude, then a message against the favoured candidate.
limits: Participants whose answer contradicted their preference were dropped (10 in Study 1).
agent_relevance: A question wording (not an instruction) is enough to impose a frame. Our schema's slot prompts are frame-carrying; word them neutrally.

source: McGuire inoculation theory and Lumsdaine & Janis (1953) background (as described in Bizer et al. 2011)
finding: Valence framing is set against inoculation: weak counterarguments pre-exposure raise resistance (McGuire & Papageorgis 1961), and two-sided messages beat one-sided ones (Lumsdaine & Janis 1953). Originals not opened.
numbers: Not available from the original papers.
limits: Secondhand description via Bizer et al. (2011).
agent_relevance: Inoculation is an effortful path to resistance; valence framing is a cheap one. Our agent wants neither; it needs frame-free items.

source: Gap note: no LLM test of support-vs-oppose valence framing found
finding: Six allowed web searches plus Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and arXiv API calls (the APIs returned 429 rate limits) surfaced no paper that runs the Bizer-Petty 'I support X' vs 'I oppose Y' manipulation on a language model. Closest work is sycophancy and prompt-wording studies, plus LLM use as a frame coder (Teeny & Petty 2025).
numbers: 0 direct LLM replications located.
limits: Absence of evidence in a limited search; other angles may find more.
agent_relevance: We may be first to measure it. Cheap test: same item as 'support A' vs 'oppose B', compare answer, stated confidence and resistance to a counter-argument.
